The client contacts one service entry point, the reverse-proxy balancer. The balancer forwards the request to a selected application server. That backend does the work and returns the response through the balancer to the client. Clients do not choose an instance themselves. The proxy adds a network hop and another component to operate.

Path-based routing of /search and /purchase to different server pools needs Layer 7. L7 understands HTTP requests and can route different paths to different backend groups, or select a backend for each request. That needs readable HTTP contents. TLS encrypts the connection, so an HTTPS proxy normally terminates TLS at the balancer to inspect the request. Encryption onward to the backend is a separate choice.

Layer 4 is the wrong unit for this split. It routes at the transport level and, for TCP, chooses a backend for a connection from network information, not from HTTP paths. Clients reuse one connection for many requests. Those requests can all reach the same backend, and adding another request on that connection does not force a new selection. One L4 connection therefore does not distribute its individual HTTP requests, and it cannot send /search and /purchase to different pools.

A balancer is unnecessary when one adequate server is enough and the service does not need traffic distribution or redundant serving. A balancer is not automatically useful in front of that single server.

evidence.quote: A load balancer distributes incoming traffic among them; a backend is a server selected to do the application work.

In this reverse-proxy example, the client contacts one service entry point. The balancer forwards the request to a selected backend. That server reads the note from the database and returns a response through the balancer to the client.
Clients need not choose an instance themselves. Distribution can use spare server capacity and support redundant serving, but the proxy adds a network hop and another component to operate.
One adequate server may be enough if the service does not need traffic distribution or redundant serving. A balancer is not automatically useful in front of it.
Routes at the transport level. For TCP traffic, it typically chooses a backend for a connection using network information, not HTTP paths.
Many note requests can reuse that connection. They can all reach the same backend; adding requests on that connection does not force new selections.
Understands HTTP requests. It can route /notes and /exports to different backend groups, or select a backend for each request.

Path routing requires readable HTTP contents. TLS encrypts the connection; an HTTPS proxy normally ends, or terminates, that TLS connection to inspect requests. Encryption to the backend is a separate configuration choice.

Round robin takes turns across eligible backends. It counts each request as one turn, so it controls an equal share of requests, not an equal share of work. A cheap seat lookup and a long request each count as one. It also does not give the stronger backend a larger share. It is a simple start only when servers and work are similar.

Least connections prefers the backend with fewer active connections. That can help when the cheap lookups and long requests make connection durations vary. Its limit is that one connection may carry far more work than another, so the connection count is not the work, and it is not a measure of the server that is twice as capable.

Weights bias the share of traffic. A server with twice the measured capacity might start with twice the weight. The limit is that configured weights are not a live measurement or a performance guarantee, and a weight does not by itself account for one connection lasting much longer than another.

For the long, uneven requests, consider least connections. For the unequal server capacity, consider weights. No policy is universally best; check actual latency and resource use before deciding.

If the shared database is saturated, another application backend alone may not raise throughput. Balancing only distributes existing capacity. More API servers help when API processing is the bottleneck. They do not remove a saturated shared database bottleneck.

After one machine fails, two things must hold. The entry path must stay reachable: a lone balancer is itself a failure point, so clients need a reachable alternate entry path, not just another disconnected balancer box. Use a managed entry or redundant frontends with working failover, and test that path. The surviving backends also need enough spare capacity for the remaining load. Otherwise redirecting traffic overloads them. Limit or reject excess work visibly instead of assuming redistribution solves it. Redundant components alone do not guarantee an available service.

evidence.quote: Takes turns across eligible backends. It is a simple starting point for similar servers and similar work; a quick note read and a slow export still each count as one request.
Prefers the backend with fewer active connections. This can help when connection durations vary, but one connection may carry far more work than another.
Bias the share of traffic. A server with twice the measured capacity might start with twice the weight. Configured weights are not a live measurement or a performance guarantee.
For long, uneven work, consider least connections; for unequal server capacity, consider weights. Check actual latency and resource use before deciding: no policy is universally best.
Balancing distributes existing capacity. More API servers can help when API processing is the bottleneck; they do not remove a saturated shared database bottleneck.

Headroom is spare capacity. After one backend fails, the survivors need enough capacity for the remaining load. Otherwise redirecting traffic can overload them. Limit or reject excess work visibly instead of assuming redistribution solves it.

A lone balancer is itself a possible failure point. If it fails, clients need a reachable alternate entry path, not just another disconnected balancer box. Use an available managed entry or redundant frontends with working failover, and test that path.
Redundant components alone do not guarantee an available service.

A health check is only a periodic sample. Readiness means the backend can accept useful new work. This process answers its health endpoint with 200 while the purchase handler cannot reach a required database, so the check does not reflect the capability needed to sell tickets. The balancer can keep selecting a server that cannot do the purchase. Use a check that fails when that required database is unreachable.

Even that improved check cannot detect every failure immediately. Checks have limited coverage, intervals, and failure thresholds. A backend can fail just after passing, and detection takes time. A green check is a sample, not a promise.

Once the failure is detected and the backend is removed from the eligible set, it stops receiving new selections. Removal does not repair requests already underway. Those requests can still fail. Removal does not complete them, undo them, or safely replay them. Health-based routing reduces exposure to the failure. It cannot guarantee every request succeeds.

evidence.quote: A health check periodically probes a backend. Readiness means it can accept useful new work: a process can answer /health while the note handler cannot reach its required database.
Use a check that reflects the capabilities needed to serve notes. Checks have limited coverage, intervals and failure thresholds; a backend can fail just after passing. Detection takes time.
Once detected and removed from eligible backends, it stops receiving new selections. Requests already underway can still fail; removal does not complete, undo or safely replay them.
A green check is a sample, not a promise
Health-based routing reduces exposure to failure; it cannot guarantee every request succeeds.

The cart is session state kept only in server A's memory. If the next request goes to B, B cannot read that cart. If A fails, the only copy can be lost with A.

Sticky routing, or affinity, prefers A for that customer's later requests. It can keep ordinary requests on A. One cost is that it skews load and restricts where the customer can be placed. It does not copy the cart, and it does not preserve the cart when A fails. Stickiness therefore does not make the cart survive A's failure.

Shared session storage lets either backend read the cart, so a request on B, or a failure of A, can still find it if the shared store is up. One cost is the extra access or coordination work and a shared dependency whose availability matters too.

Keeping the user on one server and making the cart available on another server are separate jobs. Affinity only does the first.

evidence.quote: Session state is information kept between a user's requests. If the Notes API keeps a user's session only in A's memory, B cannot read it. Losing A can lose the only copy.
Prefers the same backend for that user's requests. It can keep ordinary requests on A, but skew load and restrict placement. It does not copy the session or preserve it when A fails.
Lets either backend read the session. It adds access or coordination work and a shared dependency whose availability matters too.
Routing a user consistently and making their state available on another server are separate responsibilities.

Drain A before stopping it. First stop new assignments to A. Allow in-flight work, including the request already accepted, to finish within a deadline. The reused client connection also has to be handled: stop accepting further requests on it, or end that connection's lifetime, so it cannot keep bringing new HTTP requests. Shut A down after the accepted work completes, or when the deadline expires, whichever comes first.

New assignments are selections the balancer has not made yet. The drain stops those. The accepted 20-second request is work already underway. Draining lets that work finish inside the deadline; it is not a new assignment. When the deadline expires, forced termination may interrupt a request that is still unfinished. That work is not automatically moved to another server. Draining cannot promise zero interrupted work.

Merely stopping new L4 connections does not stop new HTTP requests on the connection the client is already reusing. Those requests still arrive on the open connection. A drain has to match the routing unit. For an L4 connection it must manage that connection's lifetime or stop accepting further requests. For L7, request-aware draining must still track work that was already accepted. Then stop the server.

evidence.quote: During a deployment, draining stops new assignments to A while allowing in-flight work, meaning requests already underway, to finish within a deadline. Shut A down after completion or when that deadline expires.

Stopping new L4 connections does not stop new HTTP requests on existing connections. A drain must also manage those connection lifetimes or stop accepting further requests. L7 request-aware draining must still track already accepted work.
Give a running note export time to finish, but bound the wait. Forced termination at the deadline may interrupt unfinished requests. Their work is not automatically moved to B.
Remove new assignments, handle existing connections and requests, then stop. Draining cannot promise zero interrupted work.

The purchase transaction committed on A, but the response was lost. The timeout means the client never saw a success or a failure, so it cannot tell whether the write committed. The committed purchase can remain stored even though the caller got no response.

A blind retry on B can create a second purchase. B does not know that A already committed this one, so it performs the write again.

Use one idempotency key, a stable ID for this logical purchase, and send that same key on every attempt. All backends share a durable database record of the key and the result. In one transaction, insert a key the database allows only once, create the purchase, and record its result. Commit all of that or none of it. A repeat finds the key already recorded and returns that result without creating another purchase. Separate check-then-write steps can race or leave a gap if the process crashes between them, so the key and the purchase have to be one transaction.

A fresh key on each retry names a different operation, so the second attempt is not recognized as a repeat. A key remembered only in A's memory is invisible to B, so the retry on B is not protected. The balancer does not make the write idempotent. The application does, with the shared record.

Retries still need a bound on attempts and a delay between them. Extra requests consume capacity and can deepen an overload. The retry policy does not replace the duplicate protection and does not guarantee that the purchase succeeds.

evidence.quote: A saves a new note, but its response is lost. The client cannot tell whether the write committed. A blind retry on B can create a second note.

A stable ID for one logical operation, reused on every attempt. Deduplication means recognizing a repeat. A new key per retry, or a key remembered only in A's memory, cannot reliably protect a retry on B.

All backends use a shared durable database record of the key and result. In one transaction, insert a key that the database allows only once, create the note and record its result; commit all or none. A repeat returns the recorded result without creating another note. Separate check-then-write steps can race or leave a crash gap.
Bound retry attempts and delay them: extra requests consume capacity and can deepen overload. Retry policy does not replace duplicate protection or guarantee success.
The application makes the effect safe to repeat; the balancer does not make an arbitrary write idempotent.
